newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian bonds open stronger after U.S. data.
newsitem.headline: Canadian bonds open stronger after U.S. data.

text.p: Canadian bonds opened stronger in steady trading on Wednesday after the release of economic data showing moderate inflationary pressures in the U.S. economy, traders said.

The U.S. Labor Department reported that the monthly Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose 0.1 percent in June compared with a 0.1 percent increase in May. Analysts said the slight increase in June was greeted favorably by bond traders.
"The U.S. CPI is fairly well supportive of the bond markets," said Harvinder Kalirai, Canadian analyst with New York-based I.D.E.A.
"There is also a little bit of short-covering continuing, and it seems like the bias is toward the upside for now," Kalirai added.
Canada's 30-year benchmark bond rose C$0.42 to C$118.90 to yield 6.550 percent.
The U.S. 30-year bond climbed 14/32 to yield 6.51 percent. The spread between the bonds widened to four basis points from a spread of two basis points at the close on Tuesday.
But a weaker Canadian dollar offset some of the gains in the bond market. The dollar opened at C$1.3727 (US$0.7285) on Wednesday after closing at C$1.3700 (US$0.7299) on Tuesday.
Analysts said U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's Humphrey-Hawkins testimony on July 22 would be the next large hurdle for the Canadian bond market.
"The next test is the Humphrey-Hawkins testimony, but until then I think we can expect bonds to push a little higher," Kalirai said.
In other prices, Canada's 10-year benchmark bond rose C$0.28 to C$109.38 to yield 5.976 percent. The U.S. 10-year bond fell 7/32 to yield 6.22 percent.
The negative spread between the two benchmark bonds was 25 basis points compared to 24 basis points at Monday's close.
The three-month cash T-bill yielded 3.21 percent against its U.S. equivalent which yielded 5.19 percent.
